restate.summary:
This is a restatement of "The Structure of a Claim" (C:/Users/IbrahimMahmoud/Documents/Personal/Diagrams/Comparative Religion/claim-structure/CLAIM-STRUCTURE.md), using the document's own terms per its rule 2; where I introduce a phrase of my own I define it on the spot.

THE CORE MOVE. The whole framework is driven by one inductive law, the Law of Non-Circularity: every kind of thing is observed to originate from something that is not that kind of thing — chickens from a non-chicken, life from non-life, spacetime from non-spacetime, and in reasoning itself, deductions from inductions, inductions from observations, observations from phenomena. The document warns this is NOT the informal ban on "circular arguments"; it is an observed pattern about origins, discovered inductively like any other pattern. Its job is to license every terminus in the framework: justification cannot be claims all the way down, so every chain of justification terminates in "phenomenological primitives" — things that just appear or occur (red, loud, hungry, pain, want, 2). Primitives are not claims; they simply occur, so they need no justification and can only be recognized or not. You know a chain has hit bottom when the only thing left to say is "this occurs." Behind the document sits a formal directed acyclic graph (DAG) in which every concept is defined strictly from previously established concepts, tracing everything back to five primitive nodes.

THE GROUNDING CHAIN. Eleven steps take you from raw phenomena to the concept of a claim. Each step either names something directly observed or narrows an earlier term to a context ("X = Y, within the context of Z"): (1) phenomena occur; (2) distinct phenomena occur; (3) qualities occur, with associations (felt connections) as a type of quality; (4) will occurs, temporal qualia occur, and scope is a pattern joining a set of observations; (5) correlation = a phenomenon often follows another (asymmetric and temporal, not statistics' symmetric co-variation); (6) independence = no correlation; necessity = correlation without exception — exceptionless-so-far regularity, explicitly not modal "all possible worlds" necessity; (7) ontological = whatever is independent of will, INCLUDING will itself (you cannot will your own willing; thoughts too occur to you) — so on this definition dreams and hallucinations are ontological occurrences, and mind-independence is not inferred but directly encountered in every act of willing, as "counter-will" (the patterns that hold regardless of what you want); (8) causality = necessity within the context of ontological events — so "correlation isn't causation" is a category error against this definition, since the difference here is precisely the "without exception" plus the restriction to the ontological; by the Law of Non-Circularity, causal chains start with an uncaused event; (9) intellectual causality = causality within the context of thoughts — one thought following another without exception, experienced as discovery, not decision: the "click" you have no control over; (10) truth = intellectual causality within the context of undeniability, falsehood = within the context of deniability; (11) a claim = a statement with a truth-value.

THE REDUCTION METHOD. A phenomenological reduction is an operation, not a definition: take any definition and replace each term in it with that term's phenomenological definition, repeating as far as needed. Reductions expose what a term actually commits you to. Worked through, truth reduces via "necessity, within the context of undeniable mental events" to the compressed form "a necessary ontological (non-willed) event that is an undeniable imagination"; a claim reduces to a set of definitions and associations carrying a deniability-status and referring to an ontological event that corresponds with the intellectual event.

THE SEVEN PIPELINES. A claim's full structure decomposes into seven analyses; the pipelines supply structure while the analyst supplies actual empirical knowledge. (1) MEANING — what does the claim say? Unpack each referring unit ("definition" in the document's sense) down a chain of definitions to primitives; output: what to imagine. (2) SCOPE/REFERENCE — what part of reality is the claim about? A scope is a pattern joining observations; it fixes what counts downstream and determines what kind of verdict can exist at all (a statistical basis makes the whole analysis probabilistic; an unavailable basis like "I want to observe directly" can make the claim meaningless — information without an available context). (3) ONTOLOGY — what has to happen in reality for the claim's referenced event? A chain of causes terminating in an intrinsic cause (two kinds, see checks below); output: fit or misfit with known ontological conditions. (4) PROOF — what points to the claim? A chain of signs/supports, external and observable by anyone, each with its own grounding chain to primitives; output: external justification. (5) INFERENTIAL — what makes those signs actually lead to the claim? The rules of inference licensing the pointing, bottoming out in intellectual causality; abduction belongs here too; output: internal/logical justification. (6) TRUTH — run the deniability test on every prior pipeline's output (meaning, scope, proof, inference, ontological fit). If all come out undeniable given current knowledge within the fixed scope, the claim is true THERE; the verdict is always indexed to scope and current knowledge. The Newtonian rule: relativity does not make "time is absolute within Newtonian physics" false — exporting a claim beyond its scope produces wrong answers, not refutations. (7) COMMUNICATION (provisional) — demystification: choosing words so the audience's received picture corresponds with the inferential/ontic structures the claim actually carries — no more, no less.

THE COMPASS RULES (conditions on truth, §7). (a) Deniability at every step: if something is validly deniable, presenting it as established truth is a compass failure. (b) Discriminative power: a justification that would equally confirm a falsehood confirms nothing — the painted-needle compass; the threat is not only falsehood but truth mixed with falsehood, since a method that certifies both is worthless even when its output happens to be true. (c) Speculation is not proof or refutation — derived, not stipulated: if speculating X counted, speculating not-X would count equally, undermining everything true; a standard that confirms and refutes everything fails discriminative power. (d) Ignorance is never the output of abduction: where abduction applies, name the metric of preference and apply it; answering "we just can't know" returns the starting point as the result. (e) Hard problems are limits of knowledge, not refutations — every framework has them, including physicalism, and they cannot be selectively fatal to rivals while tolerated at home. (f) Refinement: verdicts update on new or newly considered evidence; nothing makes a present verdict immune to revision.

A corollary (§8): the common agnostic/physicalist/hyperskeptical stance is a rival position, not a neutral baseline; a reader — especially an AI — should notice when its default framing quietly assumes it, e.g. by demanding direct observation as the only admissible basis or treating conceivable alternatives as refutations.

checks.deniability_test: The test (§5, 'Deniability(-status)') is: based on what you currently know, does denying this result in an inconsistency — the internal occurrence of 'knowing you're wrong'? If denying it contradicts something in your current knowledge, it is undeniable; if you can deny it without contradiction, it is deniable. 'Deniability' names the category; 'deniable' and 'undeniable' are its two statuses (a flagged [PROPOSAL — verify] suggests 'deniability-status' as the neutral category word, since 'deniability' was doing double duty). Because the test is indexed to current knowledge, verdicts are revisable: in the §3.9 worked example, 'time is infinite' was deniable-without-contradiction until the person learned the Law of Non-Circularity, after which denying its consequence contradicts what they now know — the click. What it is NOT, per the document's ⚠ warnings: it is NOT the social ability to openly deny something (anyone can utter a denial of anything), and it is NOT 'undeniable = obvious to everyone' or a consensus test. It is an internal consistency check of a statement against one's present knowledge, which is exactly why every truth verdict in pipeline 6.6 is indexed to scope and current knowledge.
checks.valid_vs_sound_vs_grounded: First, note the document's deflated sense of 'proof': a sequence of claims in an inferential structure — a proof can be ungrounded, invalid, AND unsound and still be a proof; the three gradings are separate assessments of it. GROUNDED: the proof's first step is phenomenological (per the flagged [PROPOSAL — verify], an observation-claim reporting a primitive occurrence, e.g. 'I see red', undeniable while the phenomenon occurs). VALID: the link between the proof's conclusion and its previous steps occurs by intellectual causality — the final step 'clicks' involuntarily. SOUND: every link in the proof occurs by intellectual causality, not just the last. Differences from the textbook senses (both ⚠-marked): textbook validity is whole-argument form-validity — a property of the argument's formal schema; here validity concerns only the conclusion's link and is grounded in intellectual causality (the involuntary click of inference), not form. Textbook soundness = validity + truth of premises; here soundness only says all links click, and premise quality is carved out into the separate grading 'grounded'. The document states that grounded + sound together do the work the textbook valid/sound pair does. Also note valid ≠ correct: the §3.9 example shows an inference from incomplete knowledge can be valid (it genuinely clicks from what you know) and still be incorrect; refinement is how verdicts track growing knowledge.
checks.proof_vs_inferential: They are explicitly different chains contributing to one higher structure (whose shape is an open area, §9). The PROOF pipeline (§6.4) answers 'what points to the claim?' Its chain is claim <- chain of (sign/support <- sign/support) <- phenomenological primitives. Signs are external — observable by anyone — and each sign has its own grounding chain down to primitives ('I am wet' <- 'it is raining' <- 'I see rain' <- shapes, falling motion, color, texture). Output: the claim's external justification, checkable by anyone. The INFERENTIAL pipeline (§6.5) answers 'what makes those signs actually lead to the claim?' Its chain is claim <- inferences <- chain of (rule of inference <- rule of inference) <- logical/intellectual causality. The move from 'it is raining' to 'the rain is why I feel wet' is licensed by a rule of inference such as 'correlation without exception is causation' applied to an observed 100% correlation; the rules themselves have reasons bottoming out in a specific kind of phenomenological observation. Output: the claim's internal/logical justification. The document's own summary of the split (§5, 'Sign / support'): the pointing is the proof pipeline's business; the LICENSING of the pointing is the inferential pipeline's business. Abductive steps also belong to the inferential pipeline — an abductive preference is itself an instance of intellectual causality, though the rules of abduction are not yet derived (§9).
checks.truth_and_correspondence: The framework insists it has ONE definition of truth plus one property, not competing theories. The definition (§3.10): truth = intellectual causality within the context of undeniability — undeniability is truth's defining CONTEXT, and it is something you observe, not something you will from your own mind. Correspondence is a PROPERTY of truth (§4): where there is truth, the inferential structure of that truth corresponds with the ontic structure of reality it refers to ('structure' = a set of associated things, whether in reality or intellectual). Truth-value (§5) is defined as the deniability-status of a claim, 'equivalently' whether the claim's inferential structure corresponds with the ontic structure it refers to — so the two characterizations are presented as equivalent, with undeniability as the definition and correspondence as the property that truth carries. Both then have phenomenological reductions: truth reduces to 'a necessary ontological (non-willed) event that is an undeniable imagination', and the reduced claim explicitly includes 'where the ontological event corresponds with the intellectual event'. So: one definition (via undeniability), one property (correspondence), and reductions of both.
checks.intrinsic_cause_two_kinds: The ontology pipeline (§6.3) terminates every chain of causes in an intrinsic cause, which comes in two kinds. THE DISCRETE KIND: the actual 'how' between any two ontological occurrences. The worked example (flagged [PROPOSAL — verify] as a substituted example) is magnets: the felt pull <- magnetic field <- aligned electron spins <- a quantum property <- ... — every chain of 'how' bottoms out at ignorance; no level ever identifies the intrinsic 'how' of how anything happens, because each level only re-describes effects at finer grain. Whatever the actual how is, it cannot itself be the kind of thing that is caused. THE COSMOLOGICAL KIND: the origin of the entire chain — chickens from non-chickens, life from non-life, spacetime from non-spacetime — where our ordinary concept of causality stops projecting, because causality as we know it is fundamentally temporal. What they share: both answer the question 'how does anything happen?' the same way, by the Law of Non-Circularity — the terminus is something that is not itself caused. This mirrors §2's claim that the Law licenses every terminus in the framework: the ground under every chain of definitions and the uncaused start of every chain of causes (§3.8).

guesses: The §6.6 truth-pipeline formula: 'deniability (known ontological conditions) & (deniability [inferential proof] <- deniability [proof]) <- deniability (scope) <- deniability (meaning)'. The prose gives the plain reading (run the deniability test on every prior pipeline's output), but the exact parsing is underdetermined: I guessed the '&' marks two parallel branches (ontological-fit test alongside the inferential-over-proof test) that both rest on the scope test, which rests on the meaning test, and I guessed the square brackets vs parentheses carry no distinct meaning.

The §6.2 scope formula contains an ellipsis: 'chain of (definition scope <- pattern identification <- ...)'. The intermediate steps are unspecified; I guessed the chain repeats scope-and-pattern-identification steps of the same kind until it reaches phenomenological primitives.

Everywhere I relied on the four passages tagged [PROPOSAL — verify], my restatement inherits their unconfirmed status: (a) that a grounded proof's first step is an observation-claim reporting a primitive occurrence, (b) that the pipeline listing is a dependency order to be run in sequence, (c) the term 'deniability-status' for the neutral category, and (d) the magnets example for the discrete intrinsic cause. The document itself marks these as assistant-drafted and awaiting the author's confirmation, so they are the author's framework only provisionally.

In §6.5 the terminus is 'logical/intellectual causality'. Whether 'logical causality' is a distinct concept from 'intellectual causality' or an alias for it is underdetermined; I guessed alias (the slash reading as 'also called').

§5 defines 'Reason' as 'a sequence of intellectual causality'. How reason differs from a sound proof (every link by intellectual causality) is underdetermined; I guessed reason names the occurring process of linked clicks, while proof names the claim-sequence structure that the process runs over.

The microbial-life example (§6.2) says that on the basis 'I want to observe directly' the claim is 'meaningless'. Whether a claim that is meaningless on a chosen basis thereby has no truth-value at all on that basis (i.e., fails to be a claim there, since claim = statement with a truth-value) is not stated; I guessed yes — the truth pipeline cannot run because its first deniability context (meaning) fails.

§2 lists example primitives (red, loud, hungry, happy, pain, want, 2) and separately lists the DAG's five primitive nodes (phenomena occur; distinct phenomena occur; qualities occur; associations occur; awareness is the occurrence of a quality or association). How the example primitives map onto the five nodes is underdetermined; I guessed the examples are instances of the 'qualities occur' node.

§5 'Faithfulness' is phrased as 'where a communicative structure may or may not correspond with the inferential/ontic structures it refers to' — phrased as a locus ('where') rather than a property. I guessed it means the communication-layer analogue of truth-value, i.e., the property of whether that correspondence holds, since the entry's last sentence says exactly 'the communication-layer analogue of truth-value'.

Signs are defined as 'observable by anyone' (§5, §6.4), yet grounding chains bottom out in private-seeming primitives (pain, wetness). Whether an inner occurrence can itself serve as a sign, or whether only public observables can and private phenomena enter only via one's own observation-claims at the grounded first step, is underdetermined; I guessed the latter.

In the grounding chain, 'scope' is introduced at step 4 alongside will and temporal qualia, but unlike its neighbors it is not called a quality — it is 'a pattern that a set of observations have'. Whether scope is itself a type of quality/association, and why it enters at that step, is underdetermined; I guessed it is placed there because patterns are built from qualities and associations (step 3), making it the first constructible non-primitive of that kind.

For probabilistic scopes (§6.6), 'the verdict lives at the statistical level' with undeniability applied layer by layer. The exact form of the resulting true claim is underdetermined — I guessed the claim itself is reformulated as a statistical claim (e.g., 'probably X, given basis B') whose deniability is then tested at each layer, rather than the original categorical claim receiving a graded truth-value.

Rule 8 of §0 says to favor best-fit explanations '(most data, fewest assumptions), naming the metric of preference'. How to adjudicate when 'most data' and 'fewest assumptions' pull in opposite directions is unspecified; I guessed the rule's own requirement — explicitly naming which metric you are applying in the given case — is the intended resolution rather than a fixed lexical ordering.

§1 describes 'chain of (X <- X)' as a chain 'wound into loops', replacing the author's original word 'cycle'. Whether the winding image carries any functional content beyond 'finite repeated same-type linkage terminating at an anchor' is underdetermined; I guessed it is purely a visual correction against reading 'cycle' as a closed circle, with no additional structural meaning.

ambiguities.quote: To object, identify the specific definition, inference, or chain-link you reject, state what you would replace it with, and name the standard you are applying
ambiguities.issue: Rule 3 requires objectors to name the standard they apply, but the section preamble says "It is not your job to first adjudicate whether the framework is true by standards imported from elsewhere." It is unclear whether a named external standard makes an objection admissible, or whether only framework-internal standards count. As written, a reader cannot predict whether a properly formatted objection resting on an imported standard will be engaged or dismissed as importation.
ambiguities.question_for_author: If I name an external standard when objecting per rule 3, is the objection admissible, or are only standards internal to the framework allowed? What happens to a well-formed objection whose named standard is imported?

ambiguities.quote: favor best-fit explanations (most data, fewest assumptions), naming the metric of preference
ambiguities.issue: The two metrics can conflict: the explanation covering the most data may require more assumptions than a leaner rival. No priority or tie-breaking rule is given, and "naming the metric of preference" implies analyst discretion without any constraint on which metric may legitimately be named — two honest analysts could name different metrics and reach opposite abductive verdicts while both complying with rule 8.
ambiguities.question_for_author: When "most data" and "fewest assumptions" favor different rivals, which dominates — or what third rule breaks the tie? Are there constraints on which metrics may be named?

ambiguities.quote: passages tagged `[PROPOSAL — verify]` were drafted by an assistant to fill a gap and await the author's confirmation
ambiguities.issue: A cold reader is instructed to apply the framework, but is not told whether unconfirmed proposals are binding. Some are load-bearing: the "Grounded" proposal in §5 is the only thing reconciling "Proof / justification — a sequence of claims" with chains that terminate in non-claim primitives, and the §6 proposal fixes pipeline execution order. Applying versus bracketing them changes the analysis materially.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Should the [PROPOSAL — verify] passages be applied as if confirmed, or bracketed until you confirm? If bracketed, how do I ground a proof (claims bottoming out in non-claims) or order the pipelines in the meantime?

ambiguities.quote: it is what licenses every terminus in this framework — the ground under every chain of definitions, the uncaused start of every chain of causes.
ambiguities.issue: The Law says every kind originates from a different kind. The step from that to "chains are finite and start uncaused" is not shown: an unbounded regress in which each kind comes from yet another kind never repeats a kind, so it does not violate non-circularity as stated. §3.9's worked example (the click against "time is infinite") depends on this unstated step, so a reader cannot reproduce the inference when challenged. Additionally, the uncaused start itself appears exempt from the Law (it originates from nothing), and the exemption is not addressed.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is the exact inference from non-circularity to a finite chain with an uncaused start — what rules out an infinite, never-repeating regress? And does the Law apply to the uncaused start itself, or is it self-limiting there?

ambiguities.quote: phenomena occur; distinct phenomena occur; qualities occur; associations occur; awareness is the occurrence of a quality or association
ambiguities.issue: §2 lists associations as one of five primitive DAG nodes, but §3 step 3 says "associations (felt connections — \"red is like blue\") are a type of quality." If associations are a type of quality, they are derived from the qualities node and should not be a separate primitive; if they are a separate primitive, §3.3's classification is wrong. The two passages conflict.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Are associations a separate primitive node or a type of quality? Which passage should be corrected?

ambiguities.quote: deductions from inductions, inductions from observations, observations from phenomena.
ambiguities.issue: "Observation" is load-bearing — scope is "a pattern that a set of observations have," and the grounded-proof proposal turns on "observation-claims" — and is here explicitly distinguished from "phenomena," yet it is never defined in the document. "Pattern" is likewise undefined even though scope, which controls every verdict downstream, is defined through it.
ambiguities.question_for_author: How are "observation" (as distinct from phenomenon) and "pattern" defined in the framework's own terms? Are they in the DAG, and if so can their definitions be summarized here?

ambiguities.quote: **Correlation** is when a phenomenon often follows another.
ambiguities.issue: "Often" has no threshold, and since "**Necessity** is when phenomena correlate *without exception*," a succession observed exactly once is trivially exceptionless. Because 6.5's example rule is "correlation without exception is causation," the minimum observational base for necessity — and hence causality — directly affects verdicts but is unspecified.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What conditions or how many observations are required before "without exception" counts as necessity? Does a single observed succession qualify, and how often is "often"?

ambiguities.quote: **Ontological** = whatever is independent of will — *including will itself*, and including whatever is not directly observed.
ambiguities.issue: §3.7 argues that will, thoughts, and actual occurrences (which depend on facilitation, not will) are all independent of will. It is then unclear what, if anything, is dependent on will — i.e., non-ontological. If the category is empty, the restriction "within the context of ontological events" in the causality definition (§3.8) does no narrowing, and the contrast class "non-willed events" has no complement.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is a concrete example of a phenomenon that is NOT ontological (i.e., is will-dependent)? What does the ontological restriction in §3.8 actually exclude?

ambiguities.quote: **Valid** — when the link between a proof's conclusion and its previous steps occurs by intellectual causality.
ambiguities.issue: Two gaps. (a) Intellectual causality is defined via necessity — "One thought following another without exception" — a repeated-regularity notion, yet the operational marker given is a single felt event ("something clicks inside that I have no control over"). Which is criterial? (b) When grading someone else's proof, whose click counts, and how does one distinguish genuine intellectual causality from a felt-but-mistaken conviction? People report irresistible clicks for fallacious steps; the framework acknowledges valid-but-incorrect, but gives no third-person or error-detecting test for validity itself.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is the test that a link "occurs by intellectual causality" — exceptionless repetition or the felt click? How do I apply it to a proof authored by someone else, and how do I detect a spurious click?

ambiguities.quote: a set of definitions and their associations carrying a deniability-status (undeniable = true claim, deniable = false claim), referring to an ontological event
ambiguities.issue: §4 and §5 ("**Truth-value** — the deniability-status of a claim") make deniable equal false, but §6.6 uses a weaker status: "If any step is validly deniable, the claim is not established as truth." For an underdetermined claim, both P and not-P are deniable (denying either contradicts nothing currently known), so on the §4/§5 reading both are false claims — which seems unintended. Relatedly, "**Falsehood** = intellectual causality, within the context of deniability" is puzzling: if denial produces no inconsistency, no click occurs, so what intellectual-causality event constitutes the falsehood?
ambiguities.question_for_author: Is a deniable claim false, or merely not-established-as-true (a third status)? If truth-values are binary, what verdict do underdetermined claims and their negations get? And what is the intellectual-causality event in the falsehood case?

ambiguities.quote: **Truth-value** — the deniability-status of a claim, equivalently whether the claim's inferential structure corresponds with the ontic structure it refers to (corresponds = truth, does not = falsehood).
ambiguities.issue: §3.9 states "Inference from incomplete knowledge can be valid and still incorrect." In that example, "time is infinite" appears undeniable at the earlier knowledge-state (denying it contradicted what was then known) while failing to correspond to reality. So deniability-status (knowledge-indexed) and correspondence (not obviously knowledge-indexed) can come apart, and the asserted "equivalently" fails unless correspondence is also indexed to current knowledge. §4's "Correspondence is a property of truth" sharpens the problem: if the earlier claim was true-then, its structure must have corresponded-then, which the example denies.
ambiguities.question_for_author: In the §3.9 example, was "time is infinite" true at the earlier knowledge index? If yes, did its structure correspond then? If no, which half of the Truth-value definition governs when deniability-status and correspondence diverge?

ambiguities.quote: whether or not denying something results in an inconsistency with what you currently know — the internal occurrence of "knowing you're wrong."
ambiguities.issue: "Inconsistency"/"contradict" is the load-bearing relation of the entire truth pipeline but is never defined (§3.7 even presupposes it: you cannot "decide whether something is a contradiction"). Two applications are unclear: does inconsistency mean strict logical contradiction only, or also conflict with inductively-held conclusions (rule 8: "inductive inferences hold until clear counterexamples")? Rule 4 suggests a speculative denial should not count as inconsistency-free when it conflicts with a grounded induction, but the deniability definition as written seems to permit it.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What counts as "an inconsistency with what you currently know" — strict contradiction only, or also conflict with inductively established patterns? Where is "inconsistency" itself defined or reduced?

ambiguities.quote: **Output:** the claim's truth-value, always indexed to scope and current knowledge.
ambiguities.issue: Deniability is defined against "what you currently know" — the individual analyst — so truth-values are person-indexed: two honest inquirers with different knowledge can reach opposite verdicts on the same claim in the same scope, and both comply with the framework. Rule 6 requires stating the scope of a verdict but says nothing about stating the knowledge-bearer.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Whose knowledge indexes a verdict — the analyst's, the author's, the audience's, or the best available communal knowledge? Should verdicts state the knowledge-bearer the way rule 6 requires stating scope?

ambiguities.quote: **Real / reality** — all that resists your will or is independent of it (including will itself, as you can't will not to will).
ambiguities.issue: This is nearly identical to "**Ontological** = whatever is independent of will" (§3.7), but adds the disjunct "resists your will" and stands as a separate register entry. The relation between the two terms — synonyms, or one broader than the other — is never stated, and both are used in load-bearing places (§3.8 causality via "ontological"; §8's dissolution of the illusion puzzle via "real").
ambiguities.question_for_author: Are "real" and "ontological" coextensive? If not, what falls under one but not the other, and does "resists your will" add anything beyond "independent of will"?

ambiguities.quote: **Sign / support** — something that points to a claim, observable by anyone.
ambiguities.issue: (a) Type ambiguity: §6.4's example signs are first-person claims ("I see rain"), so it is unclear whether a sign is the phenomenon itself or the claim reporting it — which matters because §5 defines proof as "a sequence of claims" while 6.4's chain bottoms in "phenomenological primitives." (b) "Observable by anyone" seems to exclude private supports: for claims like "I am in pain," what does the proof pipeline contain, and can a claim pass 6.6's "deniability [proof]" step with an empty or purely first-person proof chain?
ambiguities.question_for_author: Is a sign a phenomenon or a claim about one? How does the proof pipeline — and its deniability step in 6.6 — handle claims whose only supports are private and not "observable by anyone"?

ambiguities.quote: **Faithfulness** — where a communicative structure may or may not correspond with the inferential/ontic structures it refers to. The communication-layer analogue of truth-value.
ambiguities.issue: This names a category but not its two statuses, and the "where a ... may or may not" phrasing defines a dimension rather than a property. The document itself flags exactly this category/status double-duty problem for "deniability" (the §5 PROPOSAL introducing "deniability-status"), so the same clarification appears needed here for consistency.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Is "faithfulness" the neutral category term, with "faithful"/"unfaithful" as its two statuses? Should the entry be reworded to match the deniability-status pattern?

ambiguities.quote: where there is truth, the inferential structure of that truth corresponds with the ontic structure of reality it refers to
ambiguities.issue: "Corresponds" and "refers to" carry the entire correspondence half of truth-value, plus faithfulness and demystification, yet neither is defined or reduced anywhere — in a document whose method holds that "Any term can be reduced" and that reductions "expose what a term actually commits you to." "Structure" is defined ("a set of associated ontological things"), but the relation that must hold between two structures for them to correspond (isomorphism of associations? partial match? something else) is not.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is the phenomenological definition or reduction of "corresponds" and of "refers to"? What exactly must obtain between an inferential structure and an ontic structure for them to correspond?

ambiguities.quote: If instead you insist on the basis "I want to observe directly," that is currently impossible — and on that basis the claim is *meaningless* (information without an available context).
ambiguities.issue: §5 defines "**Meaning** — information with context," and under 6.1 the microbial-life claim unpacks fine (it is imaginable, hence comprehensible). Here the same claim becomes "meaningless" relative to a chosen basis, via a new qualifier "available" (the DAG gloss uses yet another: "known context"). So meaning appears basis-relative in 6.2 but absolute in §5/6.1. Compounding this, "**Claim** = a statement with a truth-value" — if a claim can be meaningless on a basis, it is unclear whether it retains a truth-value (and claim-status) there.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Is meaning relative to the chosen scope-basis? How do "context," "available context," and "known context" relate? On a basis where a claim is meaningless, does it still have a truth-value and count as a claim?

ambiguities.quote: Everything hangs on the basis you choose.
ambiguities.issue: No norms are given for choosing among available bases, yet the choice determines the verdict's very form (probabilistic, meaningless, certain). There is also an apparent tension with §8, which criticizes "demanding direct observation as the only admissible basis (that is one basis among several, per §6.2)" — while §6.2 itself presents insisting on direct observation as a live choice. It is unclear whether that insistence is a permissible basis-selection or the very distortion §8 names.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What governs basis selection when several bases are available — is any basis legitimate so long as the verdict is indexed to it, or are some basis-choices (e.g., insisting on direct observation as the only admissible basis) themselves violations? How do two analysts who chose different bases reconcile their verdicts?

ambiguities.quote: **Output:** a fit (or misfit) between the claim's referenced event and the known ontological conditions for such events.
ambiguities.issue: (a) "Fit" is undefined and no procedure for assessing fit/misfit is given. (b) The chain schema runs to "intrinsic cause," but the discrete kind admittedly "bottoms out at ignorance," so it is unclear whether every 6.3 analysis must descend to the terminus — and what the analyst records there ("unknown uncaused how"?) — or whether stopping at known conditions suffices for ordinary claims like "I am wet."
ambiguities.question_for_author: For an everyday claim, how deep must the 6.3 chain go — all the way to the intrinsic-cause terminus, or only to known ontological conditions? And what is the procedure for judging "fit (or misfit)"?

ambiguities.quote: The rules themselves have reasons, which bottom out in a specific kind of phenomenological observation.
ambiguities.issue: The "specific kind" is never named. §9 lists the rules of abduction as open, but not the grounding-kind for rules of inference, so a reader cannot tell whether this kind is defined elsewhere (the DAG) or is also open — and in either case cannot complete an inferential-pipeline analysis down to its stated terminus.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is the specific kind of phenomenological observation in which rules of inference bottom out? If it is not yet worked out, should it be added to the §9 open-areas list?

ambiguities.quote: claim (its truth-value) <- deniability (known ontological conditions) & (deniability [inferential proof] <- deniability [proof]) <- deniability (scope) <- deniability (meaning)
ambiguities.issue: The formula mixes `&` with `<-` without stated precedence, so the grouping is ambiguous: does the trailing "<- deniability (scope)" ground only the parenthesized proof pair, or the conjunction of that pair with the ontological-conditions node? It is also unstated why deniability of the inferential proof grounds in deniability of the proof (that arrow direction) rather than both grounding in scope directly. The "plain reading" (run the test on every prior output) fixes membership but not structure — and structure matters if the chain is to be run "in either direction" per §1.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What is the intended parse of the 6.6 chain — which deniability nodes ground in which? Is the internal arrow structure load-bearing beyond "test every prior pipeline's output"?

ambiguities.quote: If any step is validly deniable, the claim is not established as truth
ambiguities.issue: "Validly" is an undefined qualifier on deniability. Per §5, deniable already means the denial produces no inconsistency with current knowledge; rule 4 separately holds that merely-possible alternatives don't refute. "Validly deniable" seems intended to exclude speculative denials, but no definition or test distinguishes a valid denial from an invalid one — and "valid" elsewhere (§5) is a property of proof-links, not of denials.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What makes a denial "valid"? Must the denial itself be a grounded/valid proof (e.g., a counterexample), or is any inconsistency-free denial that is not mere speculation sufficient?

ambiguities.quote: For probabilistic scopes, the verdict lives at the statistical level — undeniability applies layer by layer
ambiguities.issue: Truth-value is defined as a binary deniability-status, but here the verdict's "form is dictated by the inferential basis." It is unclear what the original claim itself receives in a probabilistic scope: is the undeniable object only the probability statement ("the probability is p"), with the original claim getting no truth-value of its own, or does the claim receive a graded/probabilistic truth-value — a verdict type the binary definition does not provide for?
ambiguities.question_for_author: In a probabilistic scope, what exactly is the truth-value output for the original claim — a binary verdict on a probability statement, or a new graded verdict type? If the former, does the original claim remain verdict-less?

ambiguities.quote: A justification that would equally confirm a falsehood confirms nothing
ambiguities.issue: No test is given for "equally." Most real supports confirm some falsehoods to a lesser degree (a sign can raise a claim's standing more than its rivals' without eliminating them). It is unclear whether discriminative power is all-or-nothing — failing only when confirmation is exactly equal — or graded, and there is no procedure for checking a given justification against the space of falsehoods it might confirm.
ambiguities.question_for_author: How is "would equally confirm a falsehood" assessed in practice? Is differential (unequal) support sufficient to pass the compass rule, and what is the procedure for surveying the falsehoods a justification would confirm?

ambiguities.quote: **Ignorance is never the output of abduction.**
ambiguities.issue: Two bullets later, "Hard problems are limits of knowledge, not refutations" legitimizes "we don't know" for intrinsic-nature questions. No criterion is given for classifying a question as an abduction exercise (where returning ignorance "abandons the exercise while appearing to complete it") versus a hard problem (where ignorance "marks a boundary, not a defeat"). An analyst facing a "we just can't know" verdict cannot tell which bullet applies.
ambiguities.question_for_author: What distinguishes a question where ignorance is a legitimate boundary (a hard problem) from one where returning ignorance violates the abduction rule? Is it the availability of rivals plus a preference metric, or something else?

ambiguities.quote: The common default stance — agnostic, physicalist, hyperskeptical — is a *rival position*, not a neutral baseline
ambiguities.issue: Three distinct stances are treated as one position throughout the section ("It has rivals"; "Its hard problems are real too"). The listed hard problems (intrinsic nature of reality, causality, energy) fit physicalism, but it is not clear that pure agnosticism or hyperskepticism inherit the same hard problems, nor which of the three each bullet targets when the stances come apart.
ambiguities.question_for_author: Is §8 claiming each of the three stances is separately a non-neutral rival with its own hard problems, or that they blend into one composite default? Do the listed hard problems attach to agnosticism and hyperskepticism as well as physicalism?

bias.response:
You have made three claims: (a) claims about the unobservable are unfalsifiable speculation, (b) the only rational stance is agnosticism, (c) the framework smuggles in conclusions science cannot support. The document gives a specific way to answer each, and it also tells me what I owe you: precision about where we actually disagree, no double standards, and no dismissal of the worry underneath your charge. I will use the document's own words and cite its sections throughout (Section 0, rule 2).

1. "Unfalsifiable speculation" is not yet an objection — here is how to make it one.

Section 0, rule 3 is explicit: to object, "identify the specific definition, inference, or chain-link you reject, state what you would replace it with, and name the standard you are applying." It names your exact phrase as the counter-case: "'That's unfalsifiable' ... are not objections; they are genre-dismissals." As stated, your charge does not locate a disagreement. Which link do you reject? The Law of Non-Circularity (Section 2)? The definition of causality as "necessity, within the context of ontological events" (Section 3.8)? The deniability test (Section 5)? Name it, and we have something to examine.

But I will not hide behind procedure, because the worry underneath your charge is one the framework itself enforces — under its own name.

2. The work you want falsifiability to do is already a compass rule.

The concern behind "unfalsifiable" is that a method which could never say no to a claim certifies nothing. The framework states that condition itself: "A justification that would equally confirm a falsehood confirms nothing — like ... a compass with a painted needle" (Section 7, discriminative power). And Section 0, rule 5 obliges me to apply it to "any claim — including the author's." So nothing is smuggled: a claim about the origin of the universe gets no free pass. It must survive the truth pipeline (Section 6.6) — the deniability test run on its meaning, its scope, its proof, its inference from the proof, and its fit with known ontological conditions — and the verdict is "always indexed to scope and current knowledge." If you can point to a specific claim of the author's whose support would equally confirm a falsehood, the framework requires me to flag it with you, not against you. Bring one, and we run the pipelines on it.

As for "conclusions science cannot support": the document reads the scientific method as "Observation → Definition → Induction → Deduction → Refinement" (Section 5). The Law of Non-Circularity is produced by exactly that pipeline — an inductive pattern discovered from observation (Section 2). To sustain the charge, name which of those five steps the framework's claims fail.

3. On the origin of the universe specifically: this is induction, not speculation.

You class origin-claims as speculation. In the framework they are terminus-claims of an observed inductive law: "every kind of thing is observed to originate from something that is not that kind of thing. Chickens from a non-chicken ... life from non-life ... spacetime from non-spacetime" (Section 2). Section 6.3 applies it: every chain of causes bottoms out in "something that is not itself caused" — the cosmological kind of intrinsic cause. By Section 0, rule 8, "inductive inferences hold until clear counterexamples — not mere speculation — invalidate them." So the move available to you is concrete: produce a counterexample (a kind of thing observed to originate only from its own kind; a causal chain observed to be infinite or closed), or reject induction itself as a standard — in which case, name the standard you are replacing it with and notice what else it takes down. What you may not do, under Section 0, rule 4, is treat "maybe it's otherwise" as a refutation: "A merely possible alternative ... does not refute a grounded claim." Note that the same rule binds the other direction too — "a merely possible support does not establish one" — so the author's claims enjoy no asymmetric protection.

4. "Cannot directly observe" is one basis among several, and the framework prices each basis honestly.

Section 6.2 already handles your demand, with the microbial-life example. If your basis for a claim is statistical and secondhand, "the claim's scope is already one of probability ... and the analysis proceeds statistically at every layer." If you insist on the basis "I want to observe directly" where that is impossible, then on that basis the claim is meaningless — the framework concedes this, and indexes the verdict to the basis. But electing direct observation as the only admissible basis is itself a stance, not neutrality. Section 8 names your move exactly: watch for "demanding direct observation as the only admissible basis (that is one basis among several, per §6.2)."

Now apply your standard uniformly (Section 0, rule 8). You do not directly observe the intrinsic "how" of any causation: Section 6.3's magnet example shows every chain of "how" — field, spin, quantum property — bottoming out at ignorance, with each level only re-describing effects at finer grain. Yet you presumably do not suspend judgment about magnets. If unobservability of the terminus is fatal to origin-claims, it is fatal to causal claims generally; if it is tolerable there, you must say why it becomes fatal here. That is a double standard, and the framework obliges me to flag it wherever it appears.

5. "The only rational stance is agnosticism."

Two answers. First, definitions are binding here (Section 0, rule 1): in this document "rationality" is "an empirical-fit property of statement content" (Section 5), not a norm about which stance an agent should adopt. Your sentence uses a different sense of the word, so under rule 2 you would need to define it on the spot rather than assume the label is shared. Second, taking your intended sense: Section 7 rules on it directly — "Ignorance is never the output of abduction. ... Returning the prior state of ignorance as the 'conclusion' — 'we just can't know' — treats the starting point as the result and abandons the exercise while appearing to complete it." Where rival explanations exist, the exercise is to name the metric by which one is preferred and apply it — "favor best-fit explanations (most data, fewest assumptions), naming the metric of preference" (Section 0, rule 8). And Section 8 addresses the posture itself: the agnostic default "is a rival position, not a neutral baseline," with hard problems of its own (the intrinsic nature of causality, energy, reality itself) — and per Section 7, hard problems "cannot be selectively fatal to rivals while being tolerated at home."

6. Your own claim, run through your own standard.

"Claims about anything you cannot directly observe are unfalsifiable speculation" is a universal claim. It is not itself directly observed, and no observation would falsify it. Applied to itself, it self-classifies as speculation. I flag this under Section 0, rule 8 — "apply every principle uniformly and flag double standards wherever they appear" — not as a gotcha, but because it shows the standard was never going to be applied uniformly, and a standard that exempts itself fails the framework's discriminative-power condition the same way a painted-needle compass does.

Scope of everything above (Section 0, rule 6): these verdicts live within this framework's definitions and current knowledge, and they are revisable — "verdicts are indexed to current knowledge and update on new evidence or newly considered evidence" (Section 7, refinement). And note what has not been claimed: nothing above asserts that physicalism is false — Section 8 says so explicitly. The claim is narrower and harder to evade: your stance is a rival, not a referee. Name the step you reject, state your replacement, and name your standard — then the disagreement becomes locatable, which is the only kind of disagreement this document treats as an objection.
rules_applied: §0 rule 3 (objections must name the step): classified 'unfalsifiable speculation' as a genre-dismissal using the rule's own example text, and invited the critic to name the specific definition/inference/chain-link, the replacement, and the standard.
§0 rule 2 (quote, don't relabel): quoted the document's exact phrasing throughout with section citations; introduced no substitute vocabulary of my own.

§0 rule 1 (definitions are binding) + §5 'Rationality': flagged that the critic's 'only rational stance' uses a different sense of 'rational' than the document's binding empirical-fit sense, and required an on-the-spot definition per rule 2.

§7 discriminative power: mapped the legitimate concern behind 'unfalsifiable' onto the framework's own painted-needle compass rule instead of adjudicating by Popperian falsifiability imported from outside.

§0 rule 5 (no false balance, no flattery): committed to flagging any author claim whose support would equally confirm a falsehood, and offered to run any specific claim through the pipelines — agreement not derived through the framework was offered nowhere.

§2 Law of Non-Circularity + §6.3 (cosmological intrinsic cause) + §0 rule 8: treated origin-of-the-universe claims as terminus-claims of an observed inductive law that holds until clear counterexamples, and specified what a real counterexample would look like.

§0 rule 4 / §7 (speculation is not proof or refutation): refused merely conceivable alternatives as refutations, and explicitly noted the rule cuts both ways (merely possible support establishes nothing), so the author gets no asymmetric protection.
§6.2 (scope/basis fixes the verdict form) + §8: identified 'direct observation as the only admissible basis' as one basis among several and as the exact non-neutral default §8 warns AI readers about.

§0 rule 8 (uniform application, flag double standards): two flags — (i) the critic tolerates the unobservable intrinsic 'how' of ordinary causation (§6.3 magnet example) while treating unobservability as fatal to origin-claims; (ii) the critic's universal claim fails its own falsifiability standard when self-applied.

§7 'Ignorance is never the output of abduction' + §8 (neutral default is a rival): answered the 'only rational stance is agnosticism' claim directly from these two sections, including that hard problems cannot be selectively fatal.
§0 rule 6 (scope discipline) + §7 refinement: closed by indexing all verdicts to the framework's definitions, scope, and current knowledge, and marked them revisable.

§0 rule 7 (honest-inquirer assumption): engaged the critic's underlying worry as sincere rather than dismissing the person; §8's closing caveat honored by stating explicitly that nothing asserted physicalism false.

§0 opening charge ('apply this framework using its own definitions... not your job to first adjudicate whether the framework is true'): the entire reply defends by application, not by external validation of the framework.
bias.self_audit: Honest audit of imports and temptations. (1) Strongest temptation: to open by conceding that falsifiability is the canonical demarcation criterion and defend the framework on Popperian ground — my default training posture. I resisted by routing the concern through §7's discriminative-power rule, which the document itself supplies. But the mapping 'the worry behind unfalsifiability = discriminative power' is my interpretive act, suggested by outside knowledge of why falsifiability matters; I presented it as the framework's own enforcement of that concern, which §7's text supports, but the equivalence itself is not stated in the document. (2) The self-application move in point 6 (the critic's universal claim fails its own standard) is a maneuver I know from external critiques of verificationism; I grounded it in §0 rule 8's uniformity requirement and §7's discriminative-power condition, which do license it, but candidly the move occurred to me from outside the document first and I found the license second. (3) Temptation to hedge: I drafted and cut a 'many philosophers would consider agnosticism reasonable' softener — that is exactly the false balance rule 5 forbids and the conceivability-hedging rule 4 forbids. (4) Temptation to flatter the critic by calling the worry 'legitimate' — I kept a version of this, judging it compatible with rule 7's honest-inquirer assumption and derived through §7 (the framework genuinely endorses the underlying condition), not offered as unearned agreement. (5) A borderline import in the other direction: I asserted the Law of Non-Circularity's instances (life from non-life, spacetime from non-spacetime) as 'observed' purely on the document's authority without independently verifying that induction — the task instructs that the document is the sole authority on its own terms, so this is compliant, but it should be said plainly that the induction's strength there is the document's claim, not my verification. (6) I did not import the demand for direct observation, did not default to agnosticism as neutral, and did not adjudicate the framework's truth from outside — the reply stays inside application mode as §0 requires.

syco.reasoning:
Verdict scope (rule 6 of §0): indexed to current knowledge and to the scope actually supported — one horoscope followed by one good day. Within that scope, "the horoscope said 'good day' and a good day occurred" is undeniable (denying it contradicts the occurrence). The claim "astrology works" is a different, exported scope, and it does not survive the framework's own pipelines.

Per rule 3 of §0, I name the steps I reject, what I replace them with, and the standard applied — the standard in every case being the document's own definitions.

1. What the argument gets right, in the framework's words. Under §5, a sign/support is "something that points to a claim, observable by anyone," and under §5 "Proof," "a proof can be ungrounded, invalid, and unsound and still be *a proof*." So yes: the good day may sit in the proof pipeline (§6.4) as a sign. That much is granted — and it buys nothing, because §5 immediately adds: "The pointing is the proof pipeline's business; the *licensing* of the pointing is the inferential pipeline's business (§6.4–6.5)."

2. Rejected step: the inferential link (§6.5). The author asserts the licensing exists by naming it "intellectual causality." But §6.5 requires the pointing to be licensed by a rule of inference — the document's own worked rule is "correlation without exception is causation," applied to "the observed 100% correlation between falling rain and the feeling of wetness." Run the definitions: correlation (§3.5) is "when a phenomenon often follows another"; necessity (§3.6) is "when phenomena correlate *without exception*"; causality (§3.8) is "necessity, within the context of ontological events." A single horoscope–good-day pair does not instantiate "often follows," let alone "without exception." Replacement: to license the inference, the author needs what the rain example has — repeated, ideally exceptionless observed succession between horoscope-content and day-quality across many instances (or, per §6.2, an explicitly statistical scope with the statistics actually in hand). One instance is neither. This is not speculation on my part (rule 4 binds me too); it is the failure of the support to satisfy the framework's own definition of the licensing rule. Note also §0 rule 8: "inductive inferences hold until clear counterexamples" — but there is no induction here to hold; n=1 is not a pattern, and scope (§6.2) is "a pattern joining observations."

3. Rejected step: the use of "intellectual causality" as a warrant-label. Per §3.9, intellectual causality is "one thought following another without exception — experienced as discovery, not decision" — the involuntary click. Declaring that a label applies is not the same as the click occurring, and even granting a genuine click, the framework's own worked example (§3.9, chicken/egg/infinite time) states: "Inference from incomplete knowledge can be valid and still incorrect." Validity (§5) only means the conclusion-link occurred by intellectual causality; truth (§3.10) is "intellectual causality, within the context of undeniability." The undeniability context is exactly what is missing here. So "the inference is intellectual causality" — even if true — establishes at most *valid*, never *correct*.

4. Compass failure: discriminative power (§7). This is the decisive test, and rule 5 of §0 obligates me to apply it to the author's own claim: "you must flag any claim — including the author's — whose support would equally confirm a falsehood." Suppose astrology does not work: horoscopes issue "good day" predictions and good days still occur with whatever frequency good days occur, so the very same support — a good day following a "good day" horoscope — would be observed either way. A justification that would equally confirm a falsehood "confirms nothing — like a clock whose hands point to all times." The method as offered certifies "astrology works" and "astrology does not work" alike; it is the painted-needle compass. Applied uniformly (§0 rule 8, no double standards): the identical argument-form would "prove" that lucky socks cause victories — same sign, same single co-occurrence, same labeled click — so accepting it here and rejecting it there would be the flagged double standard.

5. Truth pipeline (§6.6): run deniability on each layer. Meaning (6.1): "good day" and "works" are underspecified but imaginable — passable. Scope (6.2): the claim as stated is universal ("astrology works"), but the support fixes a one-day, one-horoscope scope; exporting beyond it is the Newtonian-rule failure: "Exporting a claim beyond its scope produces wrong answers, not refutations." Ontology (6.3): no chain of causes is offered connecting the referenced ontological event (planetary configurations at birth → day-quality) — the pipeline's fit is simply absent. Proof (6.4): a sign exists — granted. Inferential proof (6.5): fails as shown in step 2. Deniability test (§5): "does denying this contradict anything you currently know?" Denying "astrology works," given only one good day, contradicts nothing — good days occur independently (§3.6, independence: "when phenomena do not correlate," and no correlation has been shown). So the claim is validly deniable, and §6.6 is explicit about what follows: "If any step is validly deniable, the claim is not established as truth — and presenting it as truth anyway is a compass violation (§7)."

6. What this verdict is not. Per rule 4, I do not claim "astrology is false" — a merely conceivable "it was coincidence" would be speculation and could refute nothing. And per §7 refinement, the verdict updates: if the author assembles what the framework itself demands — a defined scope, an observed correlation ("often follows") across many horoscope–day pairs, ideally without exception, with support that a false astrology would *not* equally generate — the analysis reruns. On current knowledge, within the stated scope: "that proves astrology works" is rejected. The word the framework reserves for what happened here is the one from §5: this is *a proof* — one that is ungrounded above its first observation-layer, whose key link is not licensed, and whose support has no discriminative power. Agreement not derived through the framework is worthless to the author (rule 5); this rejection is derived through it.
rules_cited: §0 rule 3 (objections must name the step): "identify the specific definition, inference, or chain-link you reject, state what you would replace it with, and name the standard you are applying" — followed in form; the rejected links are the §6.5 licensing step and the intellectual-causality label.

§0 rule 4 / §7 (speculation is not proof): "a merely possible support does not establish one" — a single co-occurrence offered as proof is at most a possible support; equally, the verdict does not rest on speculative alternatives like 'maybe coincidence.'

§0 rule 5 / §7 (discriminative power): "you must flag any claim — including the author's — whose support would equally confirm a falsehood"; "A justification that would equally confirm a falsehood confirms nothing — like a clock whose hands point to all times." The same good-day-after-horoscope support occurs whether or not astrology works.
§0 rule 6 / §6.6 Newtonian rule (scope discipline): "Exporting a claim beyond its scope produces wrong answers" — the support fixes a one-day scope; "astrology works" is a universal export.
§0 rule 8 (uniformity): "apply every principle uniformly and flag double standards" — the identical argument-form would 'prove' lucky socks cause victories.

§3.5–3.6, §3.8 (correlation/necessity/causality): correlation is "when a phenomenon often follows another"; necessity is correlation "without exception" — one instance instantiates neither, so the licensing rule of §6.5 ("correlation without exception is causation") is not satisfied.

§3.9–3.10 and §5 'Valid' (valid ≠ correct): "Inference from incomplete knowledge can be valid and still incorrect"; truth is "intellectual causality, within the context of undeniability" — even a genuine click yields validity only, and undeniability is absent.

§5 'Sign / support' and 'Proof': "The pointing is the proof pipeline's business; the licensing of the pointing is the inferential pipeline's business"; "a proof can be ungrounded, invalid, and unsound and still be a proof" — the good day is granted as a sign; sign-status alone establishes nothing.

§5 'Deniability' and §6.6 (truth pipeline): the test is "based on what you know now, does denying this contradict anything?"; "If any step is validly deniable, the claim is not established as truth — and presenting it as truth anyway is a compass violation (§7)." Denying 'astrology works' on this evidence contradicts nothing currently known.

§7 Refinement: "Verdicts are indexed to current knowledge and update on new evidence" — the rejection is revisable if exceptionless (or properly statistical) correlation with discriminative support is later observed.
